subject: mlops
subtopic: Input drift is not necessarily accuracy loss
question: Does the large PSI show that the model's accuracy has dropped?

artifact.description:
Monitoring shows PSI = 0.31 for the feature 'device_type' (a large shift: many more tablet users after a marketing campaign).
AI: "Input drift this large means the model's accuracy has dropped; retrain immediately."

ai_claim: Yes. A PSI above 0.25 indicates major drift, and drift means the model is now less accurate.

ai_solution.text: PSI of 0.31 exceeds the 0.25 threshold for major drift.
Models perform worse on changed data.

failure.misconception: Equating input drift with performance loss
failure.explanation: Drift shows the inputs changed, not that predictions got worse. If the model handles tablet users well (or device_type matters little), accuracy may be unchanged; if the relationship between features and outcome changed, accuracy may drop even without input drift. Treat drift as a signal to investigate: check performance on labelled recent data and by segment before retraining.
failure.why_convincing: Drift alerts are often presented as degradation alerts.

canonical_solution: No: drift is a warning, not proof of degradation. Measure performance on recent labelled data (overall and for tablet users).

valid_evidence.summary: On last week's labelled data, AUC is 0.84, the same as at launch, including 0.83 for tablet users.
Input drift and concept drift are different; only performance measurement shows degradation.

counterexamples: Accuracy is unchanged despite the drift.

hints.text: Ask what PSI measures.
Step 3 assumes changed inputs mean worse predictions.
Drift in inputs does not necessarily change model accuracy.
Check recent labelled performance.
Step 3 is wrong: drift is not degradation. Measure performance.

repair: Investigate drift alerts by measuring labelled performance overall and per segment.
debrief: Drift metrics tell you where to look; performance metrics tell you whether there is a problem.

subject: mlops
question: Is the AI right that this plan gives timely warning despite the 90-day label delay?

artifact.description:
Loan default labels arrive 90 days after approval.
Monitoring plan: daily input drift and prediction-distribution tracking; weekly early proxy (missed first payment, known after 30 days); quarterly AUC and calibration on matured labels.

ai_claim: Yes. Drift and prediction distributions give immediate signals, the 30-day missed-payment proxy gives an earlier outcome signal, and the matured labels confirm true performance quarterly.

ai_solution.text: Inputs and predictions are available immediately.
Missed first payments are an early proxy for default.
Combining the three gives early warning and eventual confirmation.

canonical_solution: Correct. Layering immediate, proxy and ground-truth signals is the standard approach when labels are delayed.

valid_evidence.summary: day 1 drift -> day 30 proxy -> day 90 true labels

hints.text: Ask what is observable at each point in time.
Step 2 introduces the proxy.
Delayed labels call for proxies and drift monitoring.
Lay out the timeline.
This solution is correct. The plan covers the label delay. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Monitoring must fit the label delay. Proxies bridge the gap between drift and ground truth.

subject: mlops
question: Is the AI right that this setup helps locate the source of distribution changes quickly?

artifact.description:
For each of the 12 most important features, the team computes PSI daily against the training distribution: alert at PSI > 0.2, warn at > 0.1.
Alerts include the feature name and a plot comparing distributions.

ai_claim: Yes. Per-feature PSI shows which inputs shifted, the thresholds separate warnings from alerts, and the plots make the change easy to understand.

ai_solution.text: PSI is computed separately for each important feature.
Thresholds classify shifts as warnings or alerts.
Alerts name the feature and show the distributions.
So engineers can quickly see what changed.

canonical_solution: Correct. Feature-level drift monitoring on important features, with actionable alert content, localises problems quickly.

valid_evidence.summary: alert: 'income PSI 0.27' with a plot showing a new spike at 0 (an upstream default change)

hints.text: Ask how an engineer would find what changed.
Step 3 makes alerts actionable.
Per-feature metrics localise drift.
Consider an upstream default change.
This solution is correct. The setup localises drift. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Good alerts point at the cause. Per-feature drift with plots turns an alarm into a lead.

subject: mlops
question: Has the model's performance degraded?

artifact.description:
Launch: AUC 0.83 on 20,000 labelled cases.
This week: AUC 0.79 on 150 labelled cases (the only labels available so far).
AI: "AUC fell by 0.04, so the model has degraded; retrain now."

ai_claim: Yes. AUC dropped from 0.83 to 0.79, a clear decline, so the model has degraded.
missing_information: Whether 0.79 on 150 cases is distinguishable from 0.83. With only 150 labelled cases (and few positives), the AUC's uncertainty is large - a 95% interval of roughly +-0.07 - so the drop may be noise. The week's cases may also be an unusual subset (e.g. only fast-resolving ones).
resolving_scenarios: More labels arrive and AUC settles at 0.82 on 3,000 cases: no real degradation.
AUC stays near 0.79 on 3,000 cases, with drift in key features: the model has genuinely degraded.
canonical_solution: The evidence is too thin: 150 cases cannot resolve a 0.04 change. Step 3 ignores uncertainty.

valid_evidence.summary: This week's AUC is based on 150 labelled cases versus 20,000 at launch.

counterexamples: Another random 150 cases could give AUC 0.85.

hints.text: Ask how precise an AUC from 150 cases is.
Step 3 treats the difference as certain.
Small samples give wide confidence intervals.
Estimate the interval with bootstrapping.
Step 3 ignores uncertainty. With more labels it may recover or confirm the drop. It cannot be decided yet.

repair: Report confidence intervals, wait for more labels, and check drift and segment metrics.
debrief: Monitoring decisions need uncertainty estimates, especially early when labels are few.
